q.s: A 45-year-old woman has had fatigue, weight loss, nausea and craving for salty foods for 4 months. Blood pressure is 92/58 mm Hg supine and 74/46 mm Hg standing. Her gums and knuckles are darkened. Sodium is 127 mEq/L and potassium 5.8 mEq/L. Plasma ACTH is 480 pg/mL. A cosyntropin stimulation test is performed; serum cortisol values are shown with a normal response for comparison.
o: Hyperpigmentation driven by increased POMC-derived MSH
e: Wrong. Renin is high from volume depletion and aldosterone loss.
Correct. Primary adrenal insufficiency (no cortisol response, high ACTH) removes negative feedback, increasing POMC cleavage to ACTH and MSH.
Wrong. Cortisol deficiency predisposes to hypoglycemia.
Wrong. Aldosterone loss causes metabolic acidosis.
cl: 92/58 mm Hg supine and 74/46 mm Hg standing
Her gums and knuckles are darkened
Hyperpigmentation of mucosa and pressure areas.
q.ch: Low cortisol with no response to cosyntropin + high ACTH → primary adrenal insufficiency → ↑ POMC → ↑ MSH (pigmentation); ↓ aldosterone → hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, acidosis, high renin.
q.tr: Primary adrenal failure: "Pigment, Potassium high, Pressure low."
q.q2: Which additional finding is most likely in this patient?

q.s: A 31-year-old man has had recurrent kidney stones and headaches. Calcium is 11.6 mg/dL with elevated PTH. Prolactin is 220 ng/mL. CT shows a 2-cm pancreatic mass, and his fasting gastrin is high. His family pedigree is shown (he is the arrow); shaded members had similar endocrine tumors.
o: A cell-cycle checkpoint protein on chromosome 17
A proto-oncogene encoding a receptor tyrosine kinase
A tumor suppressor encoding menin on chromosome 11
e: Correct. MEN1 (parathyroid, pituitary, pancreatic tumors) is autosomal dominant and caused by loss of the menin tumor suppressor.
cl: Calcium is 11.6 mg/dL with elevated PTH
pancreatic mass, and his fasting gastrin is high
q.ch: Parathyroid + pituitary + pancreas tumors with vertical (autosomal dominant) inheritance → MEN1 → menin tumor suppressor (chromosome 11).
q.tr: "MEN1 = 3 P's, on chromosome 11 (1 + 1 = 2... just remember MEN-ONE on eleven)."
q.q2: The gene responsible for this syndrome normally functions as which of the following?

q.s: An 11-year-old girl has muscle cramps and tingling of her fingers. She is short with a round face. Her 4th and 5th fingers are short, with dimples where her knuckles should be when she makes a fist. Her mother has the same appearance. Laboratory results are shown.
o: The PTH gene, producing no hormone
The Gs protein α subunit coupled to the PTH receptor (maternally inherited)
e: Correct. Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A: end-organ resistance to PTH from an inactivating GNAS mutation, with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy.
cl: Her mother has the same appearance
Maternal transmission of the imprinted GNAS mutation.
q.ch: Hypocalcemia + hyperphosphatemia + high PTH with normal vitamin D and kidneys → PTH resistance → GNAS (Gsα) mutation from mother → pseudohypoparathyroidism 1A.
q.tr: "Pseudo = PTH present but ignored"; Mother gives the disease, Father gives only the look (pseudopseudo).
q.q2: The underlying defect lies in which of the following?

q.s: A 30-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation has routine thyroid tests. She feels well and has no goiter or tremor. Her results are shown.
e: Wrong. Free T4 and TSH would be elevated.
Correct. Pregnancy (and OCPs) raise TBG, increasing total T3/T4 while free hormone and TSH stay normal.
Wrong. Lowers TBG and total T4.
Wrong. Would lower TSH and raise free T4.
Wrong. TSH would be suppressed and free T4 high.
q.k: TBG and thyroid tests in pregnancy
cl: She feels well and has no goiter or tremor
q.ch: Pregnancy → estrogen → ↑ hepatic TBG → more bound hormone → ↑ total T4/T3 with normal free T4 and TSH (euthyroid).
q.tr: "Total goes up with TBG; Free tells the truth."
q.q2: Which of the following best explains these results?

q.s: A 29-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder has polyuria. She carries a large water bottle that she refills constantly. Serum sodium is 132 mEq/L. A water deprivation test is performed; results are shown.
o: Gradual water restriction and behavioral treatment
MRI of the pituitary and replacement therapy
e: Correct. Primary polydipsia: low serum osmolality, normal ADH response and urine concentration >700 mOsm/kg with deprivation.
Wrong. Normal urine concentration excludes DI.
Wrong. Risky; can cause severe hyponatremia when intake stays high.
cl: Psychiatric illness is a common cause of primary polydipsia.
Mild dilutional hyponatremia (vs hypernatremia in DI).
q.ch: Psychiatric illness + excessive drinking + low serum osmolality + urine concentrates normally with deprivation (>700) → primary polydipsia → water restriction.
q.tr: "Polydipsia: they can concentrate; they just won't stop drinking."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

q.s: A 32-year-old woman at 26 weeks' gestation undergoes a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test. Her BMI is 33 kg/m², and her mother has type 2 diabetes. Plasma glucose values are shown with diagnostic thresholds.
o: Hyperglycemia from maternal insulin crossing the placenta
e: Wrong. Infants of diabetic mothers tend to have hypocalcemia.
Wrong. Insulin does not cross the placenta.
Correct. Maternal glucose crosses the placenta and drives fetal β-cell hyperplasia; after delivery the glucose supply stops while insulin stays high.
q.k: Gestational diabetes and infant of a diabetic mother
cl: Screening window for gestational diabetes (24–28 weeks).
Her BMI is 33 kg/m², and her mother has type 2 diabetes
One-step diagnostic test with three thresholds.
q.ch: All three OGTT values above thresholds → gestational diabetes → maternal hyperglycemia crosses placenta → fetal hyperinsulinemia → macrosomia and neonatal hypoglycemia.
q.tr: Glucose crosses, insulin doesn't: "Sugar crosses the bridge, insulin stays home."
q.q2: If her diabetes is poorly controlled, her newborn is at greatest risk for which of the following immediately after birth?

q.s: A 38-year-old woman has weight gain, easy bruising, wide purple abdominal striae, proximal weakness and new hypertension. Serum cortisol was measured every few hours over 24 hours; the profile is shown with a normal diurnal pattern.
e: Correct. Loss of the normal late-evening nadir is characteristic of Cushing syndrome; late-night salivary cortisol (with 24-hour urine free cortisol and 1-mg dexamethasone test) screens for it.
Wrong. Often normal in Cushing syndrome; the peak overlaps normal.
Wrong. Used after confirming hypercortisolism to find the cause.
q.ch: Cushingoid features → screen for hypercortisolism → loss of diurnal nadir → late-night salivary cortisol (or 24-h urine cortisol, 1-mg overnight dexamethasone test).
q.tr: "Cushing never sleeps": cortisol stays high at midnight.
q.q2: Which screening test exploits the abnormality shown?

q.s: A 42-year-old man has had hypertension and muscle weakness for 6 months. He eats several bags of black licorice candy each week. Serum potassium is 2.8 mEq/L and bicarbonate 32 mEq/L. Hormone results are shown.
e: Correct. Glycyrrhetinic acid in licorice blocks renal conversion of cortisol to cortisone, letting cortisol activate mineralocorticoid receptors (apparent mineralocorticoid excess): hypertension, hypokalemia, low renin, low aldosterone.
cl: several bags of black licorice candy each week
Serum potassium is 2.8 mEq/L and bicarbonate 32 mEq/L
q.ch: Licorice → inhibits 11β-HSD2 → cortisol not inactivated in the kidney → cortisol activates mineralocorticoid receptors → hypertension, hypokalemic alkalosis, with low renin and low aldosterone.
q.tr: "Licorice Locks cortisol ON" in the kidney.
q.q2: Which enzyme is inhibited, causing his findings?

q.s: A 43-year-old man has asymptomatic hypercalcemia found on routine testing. Calcium is 10.9 mg/dL, phosphate normal and intact PTH 58 pg/mL (normal 10–65). The 24-hour urine calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio is 0.004 (low). His father and sister have similar results; his sister had a neck operation that did not correct her calcium.
e: Correct. Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (inactivating CaSR mutation) is benign; surgery does not help.
Wrong. Does not correct the calcium and is not indicated.
cl: his sister had a neck operation that did not correct her calcium
Failed parathyroidectomy is a clue to FHH.
q.ch: Mild hypercalcemia + normal/high PTH + low urinary calcium + autosomal dominant family pattern → FHH (CaSR defect, higher set point) → no treatment.
q.tr: FHH: "Family, Hypocalciuria, Harmless."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

q.s: A 70-year-old woman who lives alone and rarely goes outside has diffuse bone pain and difficulty climbing stairs. She has a waddling gait. Radiographs show bilateral linear lucencies perpendicular to the cortex of the femoral necks. Calcium is 8.3 mg/dL, phosphate 2.4 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase elevated and PTH elevated.
e: Correct. Osteomalacia from vitamin D deficiency: low or normal calcium and phosphate, high ALP and secondary hyperparathyroidism; Looser zones (pseudofractures) are characteristic.
Wrong. ALP is high from osteoblast activity.
cl: linear lucencies perpendicular to the cortex
q.ch: Little sun + bone pain + proximal weakness + pseudofractures + low-normal Ca/phos + high ALP and PTH → vitamin D deficiency → osteomalacia.
q.tr: Osteomalacia is "soft bone": low D, low phos, high ALP, high PTH.
q.q2: Which laboratory result is most likely?

q.s: A 63-year-old man on hemodialysis has itching and bone pain. Calcium is 8.6 mg/dL, phosphate 7.9 mg/dL and intact PTH 980 pg/mL. He is already on a low-phosphate diet and calcitriol.
e: Wrong. Inhibits osteoclasts; not for CKD bone disease here.
Correct. A calcimimetic that sensitizes the calcium-sensing receptor, lowering PTH in secondary hyperparathyroidism of CKD.
q.ch: CKD → ↓ phosphate excretion and ↓ calcitriol → low Ca → high PTH (2° hyperparathyroidism) → phosphate binder + calcitriol + calcimimetic (cinacalcet).
q.tr: "Cinacalcet makes the parathyroid 'see' more calcium."
q.q2: Which drug lowers PTH by making the parathyroid more sensitive to calcium?

q.s: A 68-year-old man with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is brought in confused and dehydrated. Calcium is 15.1 mg/dL, intact PTH is suppressed and PTH-related peptide is elevated. Creatinine is 1.9 mg/dL (baseline 1.0).
o: Aggressive IV normal saline plus calcitonin and a bisphosphonate
e: Wrong. Without volume repletion it worsens dehydration.
Correct. Restore volume (promotes calciuresis), calcitonin for rapid effect, and IV bisphosphonate (eg, zoledronic acid) for sustained control.
cl: squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
Volume depletion from hypercalcemic nephrogenic DI.
q.ch: Lung SCC → PTHrP → severe hypercalcemia → polyuria, dehydration → saline first, then calcitonin and bisphosphonate.
q.tr: Severe hypercalcemia: "Saline, Salmon (calcitonin), then Bisphosphonate."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

q.s: A 36-year-old woman has a dry cough, mild dyspnea and tender red nodules on her shins. Chest radiography shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Calcium is 11.8 mg/dL, PTH is suppressed, PTHrP is undetectable and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is elevated.
o: Ectopic PTH production by lymph nodes
1α-hydroxylase activity in activated macrophages of granulomas
e: Wrong. Not consistent with the picture.
Wrong. Would raise 25-OH D rather than calcitriol primarily.
Correct. Sarcoid granulomas convert 25-OH vitamin D to calcitriol independent of PTH, increasing intestinal calcium absorption.
cl: tender red nodules on her shins
q.ch: Sarcoidosis → granuloma macrophages express 1α-hydroxylase → ↑ calcitriol → ↑ gut Ca absorption → hypercalcemia with low PTH (treat with glucocorticoids).
q.tr: "Granulomas make their own vitamin D."
q.q2: Which of the following best explains her hypercalcemia?

q.s: A 44-year-old woman undergoes total thyroidectomy for multinodular goiter. On the second postoperative day, she has perioral numbness and tingling in her fingers. Inflating a blood pressure cuff on her arm causes flexion of the wrist and fingers.
o: High calcium, low phosphate, high PTH
Low calcium, low PTH, low phosphate
Low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH
Low calcium, high phosphate, low PTH
Low calcium, low phosphate, high PTH
e: Correct. Injury or removal of the parathyroid glands during thyroidectomy causes hypoparathyroidism (Trousseau sign).
cl: Parathyroid glands may be removed or devascularized.
perioral numbness and tingling in her fingers
Inflating a blood pressure cuff on her arm causes flexion of the wrist and fingers
q.ch: Thyroidectomy → parathyroid injury → ↓ PTH → ↓ Ca, ↑ phosphate → tetany (Trousseau, Chvostek).
q.tr: "Cuff the Triceps = Trousseau; tap the Cheek = Chvostek."
q.q2: Which laboratory pattern is most likely?

q.s: A 54-year-old man has a slowly enlarging, painless, rock-hard neck mass for a year with difficulty swallowing and a feeling of tightness when breathing. The mass is fixed to surrounding tissues. He also has bilateral hydronephrosis from retroperitoneal fibrosis. Serum IgG4 is elevated. Biopsy shows dense fibrosis extending beyond the thyroid capsule with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate.
e: Wrong. Rubbery, confined to the gland.
Correct. Invasive fibrous thyroiditis, part of IgG4-related disease, mimics carcinoma.
Wrong. Pleomorphic malignant cells, rapid growth over weeks.
q.ch: Hard, fixed thyroid + retroperitoneal fibrosis + high IgG4 + fibrosis on biopsy → Riedel thyroiditis.
q.tr: "Riedel = Rock hard."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 29-year-old woman, 2 months after delivering her first child, has palpitations, anxiety and weight loss. The thyroid is slightly enlarged and nontender. TSH is suppressed and free T4 elevated. Radioactive iodine uptake is low. Anti-TPO antibodies are positive. Four months later she has fatigue and TSH of 12 µU/mL.
o: Spontaneous recovery to a euthyroid state within about a year in most women
e: Correct. Postpartum thyroiditis (a Hashimoto variant) goes hyperthyroid → hypothyroid → euthyroid; some later develop permanent hypothyroidism.
cl: 2 months after delivering her first child
Four months later she has fatigue and TSH of 12 µU/mL
q.ch: Postpartum + painless thyrotoxicosis with low uptake + anti-TPO → postpartum thyroiditis → hypothyroid phase → usually recovers.
q.tr: Postpartum thyroiditis: "Up, Down, Back to normal."
q.q2: What is the most likely course of this condition?

q.s: A newborn screening test shows a markedly elevated TSH. The 3-week-old girl is now feeding poorly, sleeps excessively, has a large tongue, an umbilical hernia, prolonged jaundice and constipation. Thyroid ultrasound shows no tissue in the neck.
e: Correct. Thyroid hormone is essential for brain maturation; congenital hypothyroidism (here thyroid agenesis/dysgenesis) must be treated with levothyroxine within the first weeks.
cl: a large tongue, an umbilical hernia, prolonged jaundice and constipation
q.ch: Newborn screen high TSH + macroglossia, umbilical hernia, jaundice + absent gland → congenital hypothyroidism → untreated → impaired brain maturation → intellectual disability.
q.tr: "Treat the newborn thyroid in 2 weeks, or the brain pays."
q.q2: Without prompt treatment, which is the most serious long-term consequence?

q.s: A 40-year-old woman from a remote mountain village has a large, smooth goiter that has grown for years. She has fatigue and cold intolerance. Several neighbors have goiters. TSH is elevated and free T4 is low. There are no thyroid antibodies.
e: Correct. The most common cause of hypothyroidism worldwide; chronic TSH stimulation produces a diffuse goiter.
Wrong. Antibodies absent; geographic clustering suggests a dietary cause.
Wrong. Not in a remote mountain area.
Wrong. Free T4 would be high.
q.ch: Endemic area + diffuse goiter + hypothyroidism without antibodies → iodine deficiency → ↓ T4 → ↑ TSH → goiter.
q.tr: "Mountains and goiters": the most common cause worldwide is iodine deficiency.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely cause?

q.s: A 39-year-old man has palpitations, heat intolerance and headaches. He has a diffuse goiter and bitemporal visual field loss. Free T4 is 3.1 ng/dL (high) and TSH is 6.8 µU/mL (high). There is no exophthalmos. MRI shows a pituitary macroadenoma.
e: Correct. Hyperthyroidism with an inappropriately normal or high TSH plus a pituitary mass indicates secondary hyperthyroidism.
cl: Chiasmal compression by a pituitary mass.
Free T4 is 3.1 ng/dL (high) and TSH is 6.8 µU/mL (high)
q.ch: Thyrotoxicosis + high TSH + diffuse goiter + pituitary macroadenoma → TSH-secreting adenoma (treat with surgery or octreotide).
q.tr: "Both high = the boss (pituitary) is the problem."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

q.s: A 47-year-old woman with Graves disease who smokes one pack daily has moderate proptosis, eye grittiness and double vision on upward gaze. She is considering definitive treatment of her hyperthyroidism and asks about radioactive iodine.
o: Radioactive iodine reliably improves the eye disease
The eye disease is caused by sympathetic overactivity only
Radioactive iodine can worsen the orbitopathy, so glucocorticoid cover (or another treatment) is considered, and she should stop smoking
Orbitopathy occurs only in hyperthyroid patients
e: Wrong. Thionamides control hormone levels but do not treat orbitopathy.
Wrong. It can worsen orbitopathy, especially in smokers.
Wrong. Lid retraction is sympathetic, but proptosis and diplopia are autoimmune infiltration.
Correct. Graves orbitopathy results from TSH receptor antibodies stimulating orbital fibroblasts (GAGs, swelling); it is treated with glucocorticoids, and smoking and RAI worsen it.
Wrong. It can occur when euthyroid.
q.ch: Graves → TSI acts on orbital fibroblasts → GAGs and inflammation → proptosis, diplopia → glucocorticoids; RAI and smoking can worsen it.
q.tr: Graves eyes "hate Smoke and RAI."
q.q2: Which statement about her eye disease is correct?

q.s: A 66-year-old woman has palpitations and weight loss. A 3-cm nodule is palpable in the right thyroid lobe. TSH is suppressed and free T3 elevated. A radioactive iodine scan shows intense uptake in the nodule with suppressed uptake in the rest of the gland.
e: Wrong. Hot nodules are rarely malignant; FNA is not routinely needed.
Correct. A toxic adenoma concentrates RAI while suppressed normal tissue is spared, so ablation treats it with low risk of later hypothyroidism.
Wrong. Autonomous nodules do not remit.
cl: A 3-cm nodule is palpable in the right thyroid lobe
TSH is suppressed and free T3 elevated
intense uptake in the nodule with suppressed uptake in the rest of the gland
q.ch: Solitary hyperfunctioning (hot) nodule → toxic adenoma (often TSH receptor activating mutation) → RAI or surgery; rarely malignant.
q.tr: "Hot nodule = Happy (benign) but hyper."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive treatment?

q.s: A 58-year-old woman has a thyroid nodule and new back pain. MRI shows a lytic lesion in a lumbar vertebra. Biopsy of the vertebral lesion shows well-formed follicles containing colloid that stain for thyroglobulin. Thyroidectomy shows a tumor with uniform follicles invading through the capsule into blood vessels; nuclei lack grooves and clearing.
o: Inactivating TP53 mutation as the initiating event
e: Correct. Follicular thyroid carcinoma spreads hematogenously (bone, lung) and is defined by capsular or vascular invasion.
cl: lytic lesion in a lumbar vertebra
invading through the capsule into blood vessels
q.ch: Thyroid tumor with capsular/vascular invasion + bone metastasis via blood → follicular carcinoma → RAS or PAX8-PPARγ.
q.tr: "Follicular goes through the blood (Follows the vessels)."
q.q2: Which genetic change is most associated with this tumor?

q.s: An 80-year-old woman with a long-standing nodular goiter has a neck mass that has grown rapidly over 3 weeks, with hoarseness, dysphagia and stridor. The mass is hard and fixed. Biopsy shows bizarre pleomorphic giant and spindle cells with many mitoses; thyroglobulin staining is negative.
o: It responds well to radioactive iodine
It often arises from dedifferentiation of a pre-existing well-differentiated carcinoma and carries a very poor prognosis
It typically affects children after radiation
e: Wrong. Dedifferentiated cells do not concentrate iodine.
Correct. Anaplastic carcinoma occurs in older adults, grows rapidly with compressive symptoms and is usually fatal within months.
cl: bizarre pleomorphic giant and spindle cells
q.ch: Elderly + rapidly enlarging hard neck mass + compression + pleomorphic cells → anaplastic carcinoma (dedifferentiation, p53) → very poor prognosis.
q.tr: "Anaplastic = Aggressive, Aged, Awful prognosis."
q.q2: Which statement about this tumor is correct?

q.s: After total thyroidectomy for papillary carcinoma, a 45-year-old teacher has a weak, breathy, hoarse voice and coughs when drinking liquids. Laryngoscopy shows the left vocal cord fixed in a paramedian position.
o: Left recurrent laryngeal nerve; inferior thyroid artery
Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve; superior laryngeal artery
External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve; superior thyroid artery
Vagus nerve trunk; common carotid artery
e: Correct. The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs near the inferior thyroid artery; injury paralyzes intrinsic laryngeal muscles (except cricothyroid), causing hoarseness and aspiration.
Wrong. Sensory loss above the cords.
Wrong. Causes loss of high-pitched voice, not cord paralysis.
Wrong. Not the classic thyroidectomy injury.
cl: left vocal cord fixed in a paramedian position
q.ch: Thyroidectomy → recurrent laryngeal nerve injured near the inferior thyroid artery → ipsilateral cord paralysis → hoarseness and aspiration.
q.tr: "Recurrent laryngeal runs with the Inferior thyroid artery: Inferior = Injury to voice."
q.q2: Which nerve was injured, and during ligation of which vessel?

q.s: A 70-year-old man has been in the ICU for 10 days with septic shock and respiratory failure. He has no history of thyroid disease. Free T3 is low, reverse T3 is high, free T4 is low-normal and TSH is 0.6 µU/mL. He is on norepinephrine and high-dose hydrocortisone.
o: No thyroid treatment; repeat tests after recovery
e: Correct. Nonthyroidal illness (euthyroid sick) syndrome reflects reduced 5′-deiodinase activity from illness and glucocorticoids; it resolves with recovery.
Wrong. Not beneficial in nonthyroidal illness.
cl: Shift of T4 metabolism to inactive rT3.
q.ch: Critical illness + glucocorticoids → ↓ 5′-deiodinase → ↓ T3, ↑ rT3, normal/low TSH → euthyroid sick syndrome → no treatment.
q.tr: "Sick euthyroid: low T3, high reverse T3 — treat the illness, not the labs."
q.q2: Which of the following is the most appropriate management of these thyroid tests?

q.s: A 35-year-old woman has Cushing syndrome. ACTH is elevated, cortisol suppresses with high-dose dexamethasone, and a 6-mm pituitary adenoma is seen on MRI. Inferior petrosal sinus sampling confirms a central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient.
o: Transsphenoidal resection of the pituitary adenoma
e: Wrong. Used as a bridge or when surgery fails.
Wrong. Reserved for failure of pituitary surgery; risks Nelson syndrome.
Correct. Cushing disease is treated by removing the corticotroph adenoma.
q.ch: ACTH-dependent Cushing + high-dose suppression + pituitary adenoma + IPSS gradient → Cushing disease → transsphenoidal surgery.
q.tr: Cushing DISEASE = pituitary; Cushing SYNDROME = any cause.
q.q2: Which of the following is the treatment of choice?

q.s: A 41-year-old woman had bilateral adrenalectomy 3 years ago for Cushing disease that persisted after pituitary surgery. She takes hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. She now has progressive darkening of her skin, headaches and bitemporal visual field loss. ACTH is markedly elevated.
o: Ectopic ACTH from a new lung tumor
Rapid growth of the pituitary corticotroph adenoma after loss of cortisol feedback (Nelson syndrome)
e: Correct. Removing both adrenals eliminates negative feedback, so the ACTH-secreting adenoma enlarges, causing hyperpigmentation and mass effect.
Wrong. Does not explain visual loss.
Wrong. Would cause recurrent Cushing, not hyperpigmentation with visual loss.
cl: bilateral adrenalectomy 3 years ago for Cushing disease
Loss of cortisol feedback on a corticotroph adenoma.
q.ch: Bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing disease → no cortisol feedback → corticotroph adenoma grows → very high ACTH (pigmentation) + chiasm compression → Nelson syndrome.
q.tr: "Nelson = No adrenals, Enlarging pituitary, Lots of pigment."
q.q2: Which of the following best explains her findings?

q.s: A 3-year-old girl has pubic hair, acne, clitoral enlargement and rapid growth. Blood pressure is 148/96 mm Hg. Serum potassium is 3.2 mEq/L. Plasma renin activity is suppressed, and 11-deoxycortisol and 11-deoxycorticosterone are elevated.
e: Wrong. Salt wasting with high renin.
Correct. Accumulated 11-deoxycorticosterone (a mineralocorticoid) causes hypertension, hypokalemia and low renin; androgen excess causes virilization.
q.ch: Virilization + hypertension + low renin + ↑ 11-deoxycorticosterone and 11-deoxycortisol → 11β-hydroxylase deficiency.
q.tr: 11β starts AND ends with 1: hypertension AND virilization.
q.q2: Which enzyme is deficient?

q.s: A 16-year-old phenotypic girl has primary amenorrhea and no breast development. She has no pubic or axillary hair. Blood pressure is 158/100 mm Hg and potassium 2.9 mEq/L. A pelvic ultrasound shows no uterus, and karyotype is 46,XY with intra-abdominal testes.
e: Wrong. Breasts develop and blood pressure is normal.
Correct. Blocked cortisol and sex steroid synthesis; excess 11-deoxycorticosterone causes hypertension and hypokalemia; XY individuals have female-appearing genitalia and no puberty.
Wrong. Normal blood pressure; virilization at puberty.
q.ch: 46,XY with female phenotype + absent puberty + hypertension and hypokalemia → 17α-hydroxylase deficiency (↓ sex steroids and cortisol, ↑ DOC).
q.tr: 17α "starts with 1" (hypertension) but doesn't end with 1 (no virilization).
q.q2: Which enzyme deficiency best explains her findings?

q.s: A 52-year-old man with bipolar disorder has taken lithium for 15 years. He has polyuria and nocturia. Serum sodium is 147 mEq/L. Urine osmolality does not rise with water deprivation or after desmopressin. His psychiatrist wants to continue lithium.
e: Wrong. Blocks ADH and worsens polyuria.
Correct. Lithium enters collecting duct cells through ENaC and causes nephrogenic DI; amiloride blocks ENaC, limiting lithium entry and reducing urine output.
Wrong. The kidney is resistant to ADH.
cl: does not rise with water deprivation or after desmopressin
Need a treatment compatible with lithium.
q.ch: Lithium → enters principal cells via ENaC → ADH resistance → nephrogenic DI → amiloride blocks ENaC (also thiazides, low-solute diet).
q.tr: "Lithium gets in through ENaC — Amiloride locks the door."
q.q2: Which drug is the best choice to reduce his polyuria?

q.s: A 34-year-old woman with epilepsy started a new antiseizure medication 3 weeks ago. She now has headache and confusion. Serum sodium is 121 mEq/L, serum osmolality 254 mOsm/kg and urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg. She is euvolemic. TSH and cortisol are normal.
e: Correct. Carbamazepine (and oxcarbazepine) causes SIADH, as do SSRIs and cyclophosphamide.
cl: started a new antiseizure medication 3 weeks ago
q.ch: Euvolemic hyponatremia + concentrated urine + normal thyroid/adrenal + new antiepileptic → SIADH → carbamazepine.
q.tr: SIADH drugs: "Can't Sit (carbamazepine, SSRIs, cyclophosphamide)."
q.q2: Which drug most likely caused her hyponatremia?

q.s: A 9-year-old boy has headaches, has fallen behind in growth for 2 years and drinks large amounts of water. He bumps into objects on both sides. MRI shows a cystic suprasellar mass with calcifications filled with fluid that looks like "machinery oil."
e: Correct. Craniopharyngioma arises from Rathke pouch epithelium (oral ectoderm); it compresses the chiasm and pituitary/hypothalamus (GH deficiency, DI).
cl: fallen behind in growth for 2 years
bumps into objects on both sides
q.ch: Child + growth failure + DI + bitemporal field loss + calcified cystic suprasellar mass → craniopharyngioma → Rathke pouch remnant.
q.tr: "Craniopharyngioma = Calcified, Cystic, Child, Rathke."
q.q2: From which embryologic structure does this tumor arise?

q.s: A 7-year-old boy with a history of poor feeding and hypotonia as an infant now eats constantly, takes food from the trash and has severe obesity. He has short stature, small hands and feet and hypogonadism. Genetic testing shows loss of the paternally inherited 15q11–q13 region.
e: Correct. Prader-Willi syndrome features very high ghrelin, which stimulates hunger via the lateral hypothalamus.
Wrong. Leptin is high with obesity; this is not leptin deficiency.
cl: poor feeding and hypotonia as an infant
eats constantly, takes food from the trash
loss of the paternally inherited 15q11–q13 region
q.ch: Paternal 15q11–13 loss → Prader-Willi → ↑ ghrelin → hyperphagia and obesity.
q.tr: "Ghrelin makes you ghrow hunghry" — very high in Prader-Willi.
q.q2: Which hormone is elevated and drives his hyperphagia?

q.s: A 59-year-old woman has a painful, red, blistering rash that migrates over her groin and buttocks, with crusting at the edges. She has lost 9 kg, has new diabetes, diarrhea and depressed mood, and had a deep vein thrombosis 2 months ago. A 4-cm pancreatic tail mass is seen on CT.
e: Correct. Glucagonoma: necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes, DVT, weight loss, depression, diarrhea (6 D's).
cl: red, blistering rash that migrates over her groin and buttocks
q.ch: Necrolytic migratory erythema + diabetes + DVT + weight loss + depression + diarrhea + pancreatic mass → glucagonoma (α cells).
q.tr: Glucagonoma's 6 D's: Dermatitis, Diabetes, DVT, Declining weight, Depression, Diarrhea.
q.q2: The tumor most likely arises from which cell type?

q.s: A 62-year-old man has new diabetes, foul-smelling greasy stools and episodes of right upper quadrant pain. Ultrasonography shows gallstones. Gastric analysis shows very low acid output. CT shows a pancreatic head mass, and plasma levels of a hormone from pancreatic δ cells are markedly elevated.
o: Excess gastrin causing acid inactivation of lipase
Bile duct obstruction by gallstones alone
Inhibition of cholecystokinin and secretin release
e: Wrong. Does not explain the full picture.
Correct. Somatostatinoma suppresses CCK and secretin (poor pancreatic enzymes and bicarbonate, gallbladder stasis → stones), insulin (diabetes) and gastrin (achlorhydria).
q.ch: δ-cell tumor → excess somatostatin → ↓ CCK, secretin, insulin, gastrin → steatorrhea, gallstones, diabetes, achlorhydria.
q.tr: Somatostatin "Stops everything": Stones, Steatorrhea, Sugar (diabetes), no acid.
q.q2: Which of the following best explains his steatorrhea?

q.s: A 21-year-old man with a tall, thin build and long limbs has bumpy nodules on his lips and tongue. He has a firm thyroid nodule and an elevated calcitonin. Plasma metanephrines are elevated. He has never had hypercalcemia.
e: Correct. Medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas and marfanoid habitus (RET mutation).
Wrong. Includes parathyroid hyperplasia and lacks mucosal neuromas.
cl: tall, thin build and long limbs
bumpy nodules on his lips and tongue
q.ch: Marfanoid + mucosal neuromas + MTC + pheochromocytoma, no hyperparathyroidism → MEN2B (RET).
q.tr: MEN2B = "1 P (pheo), 2 M's (MTC, mucosal neuromas)."
q.q2: Which syndrome best explains his findings?

q.s: A 67-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is started on a new oral agent to improve insulin sensitivity. Six weeks later, she has gained 4 kg and has worsening leg edema, orthopnea and crackles.
e: Wrong. Does not cause fluid retention.
Wrong. Causes weight gain but not this degree of fluid retention.
Correct. PPAR-γ agonists cause fluid retention, weight gain and worsening heart failure (and fractures).
cl: heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
worsening leg edema, orthopnea and crackles
q.ch: Insulin sensitizer + weight gain, edema, HF decompensation → pioglitazone (PPAR-γ: renal sodium retention).
q.tr: "Glitazones Gain fluid."
q.q2: Which drug was most likely started?

q.s: A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 18 years has burning pain and numbness in both feet in a stocking distribution and blurred vision from cataracts. Ankle reflexes are absent and vibration sense is reduced.
o: Accumulation of sorbitol in cells with aldose reductase and little sorbitol dehydrogenase
e: Correct. Hyperglycemia drives the polyol pathway; sorbitol accumulates osmotically in Schwann cells, lens and retina.
Wrong. Possible on metformin but does not explain cataracts.
cl: Ankle reflexes are absent and vibration sense is reduced
q.ch: Chronic hyperglycemia → aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol → tissues with low sorbitol dehydrogenase (nerves, lens, retina, kidney) swell osmotically → neuropathy and cataracts.
q.tr: "Sorbitol Swells Schwann cells and lenses."
q.q2: Which mechanism contributes to his nerve and lens damage?

q.s: A 68-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has taken metformin for 12 years. She has fatigue, unsteady gait and tingling in her feet. Hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL with an MCV of 112 fL. Vibration and position sense are reduced in the feet, and Romberg sign is positive.
o: Serum vitamin B12 with elevated methylmalonic acid
e: Correct. Long-term metformin reduces B12 absorption, causing megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration (elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine).
Wrong. Copper deficiency can mimic this but metformin points to B12.
Wrong. Folate deficiency causes macrocytosis but not posterior column signs.
q.ch: Long-term metformin → ↓ ileal B12 absorption → megaloblastic anemia + subacute combined degeneration → low B12, high methylmalonic acid.
q.tr: "Metformin Makes B12 Missing."
q.q2: Which test is most likely abnormal?

q.s: A 49-year-old man with alcohol use disorder is admitted with muscle cramps and a seizure. Calcium is 6.8 mg/dL, albumin is normal, phosphate is normal and magnesium is 0.7 mg/dL. Intact PTH is inappropriately low. Intravenous calcium gluconate raises his calcium only briefly.
e: Correct. Severe hypomagnesemia suppresses PTH secretion and causes PTH resistance; calcium will not normalize until magnesium is repleted.
Wrong. Does not correct the underlying problem.
cl: PTH secretion is suppressed by very low Mg2+.
Refractory hypocalcemia until Mg2+ is replaced.
q.ch: Alcohol → severe ↓ Mg2+ → ↓ PTH release and action → refractory hypocalcemia → replace magnesium first.
q.tr: "Mg first, then Ca": low magnesium locks the parathyroid.
q.q2: Which of the following is the most important next step to correct his hypocalcemia?
